decks.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division — Part 1: The cell cycle and mitosis
goals: Describe the events of the G1, S and G2 phases and draw the cell cycle
Identify the stages of mitosis from a diagram or slide and describe what happens to the chromosomes
Distinguish cytokinesis in plant cells (cell plate) from animal cells (furrowing)

slides.heading: Cell Cycle, Cell Division and Chromosomes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides into two identical cells.

visual.alt: Flow of the cell cycle: interphase, then karyokinesis, then cytokinesis, and back to interphase

slides.narration: You began life as a single cell. Today your body has trillions. Every one of those cells came from an earlier cell by division. In this part we follow one cell through its life: growing, copying its genetic material, and splitting into two.

slides.heading: The cell cycle
slides.body_md: The **cell cycle** is the sequence of events from the formation of a cell to its own division. It has **interphase** (G1, S, G2) and the **M phase** (mitosis and cytokinesis).

slides.narration: Think of the cycle as a clock. Most of the time the cell is in interphase, which has three parts. Only a short part of the cycle is spent actually dividing. When the division ends, each new cell starts the cycle again.

slides.heading: What happens in interphase

rows: Cell grows; makes proteins and new organelles
DNA is copied; each chromosome now has two chromatids
Cell makes proteins for the spindle and gets ready to divide

visual.alt: Table of the three phases of interphase and their main events

slides.narration: Interphase is not a resting stage. In the first gap the cell grows. In the synthesis phase it makes an exact copy of all its DNA. In the second gap it builds the materials it will need for division.

slides.heading: Quick check: copying DNA
slides.body_md: In which phase is the DNA copied?
slides.narration: Remember what the letter S stands for.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: DNA through the cycle
slides.body_md: Take the DNA in a gamete as 1 unit (C).
bullets: Step 1: a body cell in G1 has **2C**.
Step 2: after the S phase it has **4C**.
Step 3: each daughter cell after mitosis has **2C** again.

visual.alt: Table of DNA content: two units in G1, four after the S phase and in G2, two in each daughter cell, one in a gamete

slides.narration: The amount of DNA doubles in the synthesis phase and is then shared equally between the two daughter cells. So each new cell has exactly as much DNA as its parent had before copying.

slides.body_md: **Mitosis** divides the nucleus into two identical nuclei in four stages: **prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase**.

slides.narration: Here is an animal cell with four chromosomes. In prophase they thicken and the nuclear membrane fades. In metaphase they line up across the middle. In anaphase their halves are pulled apart. In telophase two new nuclei form.

slides.heading: What happens in each stage

rows: Chromatin condenses into chromosomes of two chromatids; nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear; centrioles move to the poles and the spindle forms
Chromosomes line up on the equator; each centromere is attached to spindle fibres from both poles
Centromeres split; sister chromatids move to opposite poles
Chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil; nuclear membranes and nucleoli re-form

visual.alt: Table of the four stages of mitosis and what is seen in each

slides.narration: Learn each stage by what the chromosomes are doing. Thickening, lining up, separating, and arriving. Telophase is almost prophase played backwards.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming the stage
slides.body_md: An onion root-tip slide shows these cells. Name the stage.
bullets: Step 1: look for the **nuclear membrane**: present or absent?
Step 2: look at the **chromosomes**: threads, a single row, or two moving groups?
Step 3: name the stage.

rows: Chromosomes in one row across the middle
Two groups of V-shaped chromosomes moving apart
Two groups at the ends; new membranes forming

visual.alt: Worked table matching four slide descriptions to the stages prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase

slides.narration: When you see a slide, ask two questions. Is there a nuclear membrane? And what are the chromosomes doing? A single row means metaphase. Two groups moving apart means anaphase.

slides.heading: Quick check: separating chromatids
slides.body_md: True or false: in anaphase each chromosome splits at its centromere.
slides.narration: What holds the two chromatids together, and when does it split?

slides.narration: After the nucleus divides, the cytoplasm must be shared. An animal cell pinches in from the outside, like a balloon squeezed in the middle. A plant cell cannot do this because of its wall, so it builds a new wall from the centre outwards.

slides.heading: Quick check: the cell plate
slides.body_md: Why does a plant cell form a cell plate?
slides.narration: Think about what surrounds a plant cell.

slides.heading: Where mitosis happens

rows: A seedling grows taller; a baby grows into an adult
A cut in the skin heals
Old red blood cells and gut lining cells are replaced
Amoeba splits; potato tubers give new plants

visual.alt: Table of four uses of mitosis with examples

slides.narration: Mitosis happens wherever new, identical cells are needed: in growing root and shoot tips, in healing skin, in bone marrow and in many single-celled organisms that reproduce by splitting.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2) plus M phase.
DNA is copied in the S phase.
Mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.
Cytokinesis: furrow in animal cells, cell plate in plant cells.
Mitosis gives two identical cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

visual.alt: Summary table of one key word for each stage of mitosis

slides.narration: To recap. A cell spends most of its life in interphase, copying its DNA in the synthesis phase. Mitosis then shares the copies equally in four stages, and cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Do not call interphase a **resting** stage: the cell is very active.
For diagrams, show **chromatids** joined at a **centromere** in prophase and metaphase.
Plant cells: **cell plate**, **no centrioles**. Animal cells: **furrow**, **centrioles**.
Give the stage **and** the evidence when identifying from a slide.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Interphase is busy, not resting. Draw chromatids and centromeres neatly. Remember the plant and animal differences. And when you name a stage, say what you saw that told you.

decks.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division — Part 2: Meiosis and the chromosome
goals: Explain why meiosis halves the chromosome number and how crossing over produces variation
Tabulate the differences between mitosis and meiosis and state the significance of each
Draw and label a chromosome and relate DNA, genes, chromatin and chromosomes

slides.heading: Meiosis and the Chromosome
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the division that makes gametes, and what a chromosome is made of.

visual.alt: Flow: diploid parent cells undergo meiosis to form haploid gametes, which fuse at fertilisation to form a diploid zygote

slides.narration: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same. But eggs and sperms must carry only half. Meiosis is the special division that makes this possible, and it also mixes genes so that every child is unique.

slides.heading: Why meiosis halves the number
slides.body_md: **Meiosis** is a **reduction division**: one diploid (2n) cell gives **four haploid (n)** cells.

visual.alt: Table of human chromosome numbers: body cell forty-six, sperm or egg twenty-three, zygote forty-six

Variation is the raw material of evolution

slides.heading: Worked example 2: chromosomes or chromatids?
slides.body_md: Count carefully at each stage in a human cell.
bullets: Step 1: before the S phase, each chromosome is a **single** thread.
Step 2: after the S phase, each has **two chromatids**.
Step 3: in anaphase the chromatids separate and each is counted as a **chromosome**.

slides.body_md: Which part holds the sister chromatids together?
slides.narration: It is also where the spindle fibres attach.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: four haploid gametes from one diploid cell.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes produces variation.
Mitosis: growth and repair. Meiosis: constant number and variation.
Chromosome: two chromatids, centromere; DNA with genes, packed as chromatin.

rows: Matching chromosomes, one from each parent
One of two copies of a chromosome
Segment of DNA for a character

visual.alt: Summary table of three key terms

slides.narration: To recap. Meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosomes and mixes genes by crossing over. Mitosis grows and repairs the body. And every chromosome is DNA, carrying genes, packed into two chromatids at division.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Stages of meiosis are **not** in your syllabus: learn its **purpose**, **reduction** and **crossing over**.
In difference tables, write **matching points** side by side.
Count **centromeres** to count chromosomes.
Label diagrams with **ruled lines** and neat print.
slides.narration: Exam tips. You do not need the stages of meiosis, but you must explain why it halves the number and how crossing over causes variation. Write differences point against point, count chromosomes by their centromeres, and label diagrams neatly.

sections.heading: 1. The cell cycle
sections.body_md:
**Cell cycle.** The sequence of events by which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides into two daughter cells. It has two parts:
- **Interphase** — the longest part; the cell is very active (not "resting").
  - **G1 (first gap):** the cell grows, makes proteins and new organelles.
  - **S (synthesis):** the **DNA is replicated**; each chromosome now consists of **two sister chromatids**.
  - **G2 (second gap):** the cell makes proteins for the spindle and prepares to divide.
- **M phase** — **karyokinesis** (division of the nucleus by mitosis) followed by **cytokinesis** (division of the cytoplasm).

**DNA content** (taking a gamete as 1C): G1 2C → after S 4C → each daughter cell 2C.

**Cell division** is needed for growth, repair, replacement of cells and reproduction.

The stage between two divisions, made of G1, S and G2.
The phase in which DNA is replicated.

sections.heading: 2. Mitosis and cytokinesis
sections.body_md:
**Mitosis** is the division of the nucleus that gives **two daughter nuclei identical** to the parent nucleus, with the **same chromosome number**. It occurs in **somatic (body) cells**, especially in meristems (root and shoot tips), skin and bone marrow.

| Stage | Events |
|---|---|
| **Prophase** | Chromatin condenses into chromosomes, each of two chromatids joined at a centromere; nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear; in animal cells the centrioles move to opposite poles and the spindle forms |
| **Metaphase** | Chromosomes line up on the **equator** (metaphase plate); each centromere is attached to spindle fibres from both poles; chromosomes are most distinct |
| **Anaphase** | Centromeres split; **sister chromatids separate** and are pulled to **opposite poles** (V-shaped, centromere leading) |
| **Telophase** | Chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil; **nuclear membrane and nucleolus re-form**; two nuclei |

**Cytokinesis**
- **Animal cell:** a **furrow** (cleavage) in the cell membrane deepens from **outside inwards** and divides the cell.
- **Plant cell:** vesicles join at the centre to form a **cell plate**, which grows **outwards**; a new cell wall forms. Higher plant cells have **no centrioles**; the spindle forms from the polar cytoplasm.

key_terms.definition_md: Nuclear division giving two identical nuclei with the same chromosome number.
The partition formed at the centre of a dividing plant cell that becomes the new wall.

sections.heading: 3. Meiosis, homologous chromosomes and crossing over
sections.body_md:
**Meiosis** is the division that forms **gametes** (sperms, eggs, pollen, ova). One **diploid (2n)** cell divides to give **four haploid (n)** cells, so it is called a **reduction division**. (The stages of meiosis are not in the syllabus.)

**Why halve the number?** At fertilisation two gametes fuse. Haploid gametes give a diploid zygote, so the chromosome number stays **constant** from generation to generation (human: 46 → 23 in gametes → 46 in zygote).

**Homologous chromosomes** are a pair of chromosomes alike in size and shape, carrying genes for the same characters at the same positions — **one from the father, one from the mother**.

**Crossing over.** During meiosis homologous chromosomes pair up; **non-sister chromatids** cross at points called **chiasmata** and **exchange segments**. The chromatids then carry **new combinations of genes**. Together with the random sorting of chromosomes into gametes, this produces **variation**.

sections.heading: 4. Significance of mitosis and meiosis; differences
sections.body_md:
**Significance of mitosis:** growth of a multicellular organism from a zygote; repair of wounds and regeneration; replacement of worn-out cells (red blood cells, skin, gut lining); asexual reproduction (amoeba, vegetative propagation); keeps the genetic material **unchanged** in body cells.

**Significance of meiosis:** forms **gametes**; keeps the chromosome number **constant** across generations; produces **variation**, the raw material of evolution.

| Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|
| Somatic cells | Reproductive cells (gamete formation) |
| Two daughter cells | Four daughter cells |
| Chromosome number unchanged (2n → 2n) | Chromosome number halved (2n → n) |
| No crossing over | Crossing over occurs |
| Daughter cells identical | Daughter cells genetically different |

key_terms.definition_md: Having two sets of chromosomes, as in body cells.
Having one set of chromosomes, as in gametes.

sections.heading: 5. Structure of a chromosome
sections.body_md:
**Chromosomes** are thread-like structures in the nucleus that carry hereditary information. Humans have **46** (23 pairs) in each body cell.

- **Chromatin:** in a non-dividing nucleus the genetic material is a fine network of **DNA wound around proteins**. During division it coils into compact chromosomes.
- **Chromatids:** after the S phase each chromosome has **two identical sister chromatids**.
- **Centromere:** the narrow region that **holds the chromatids together** and to which **spindle fibres attach**.
- **DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid):** a long **double helix** that carries the **coded genetic instructions**.
- **Gene:** a **segment of DNA** at a particular position on a chromosome that controls a particular character; genes are arranged in a **linear** order.

**Relationship:** genes are parts of DNA; DNA with proteins forms chromatin; chromatin coils to form a chromosome.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling interphase a "resting stage".
- Doubling the chromosome number at metaphase: it is the **chromatids** that double (46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids in a human cell).
- Drawing centrioles in plant cells, or a cell plate in animal cells.
- Writing stages of meiosis (not in the syllabus) instead of its purpose.
- Saying meiosis forms two cells, or that its products are identical.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a stage, an odd one out **with its category**, a chromosome number.
- 2 marks: two reasons or two differences, each matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a neat, labelled diagram (stage of mitosis, chromosome, crossing over) — one mark each for the drawing, its key features and correct labels.

questions.stem_md: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA of a cell copied?
questions.solution_md: DNA replication (synthesis) takes place in the S phase of interphase — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A freshly formed daughter cell in a growing root tip increases in size and makes new proteins and organelles. It is in
questions.solution_md: Growth and protein synthesis right after division happen in G1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: If you look at hundreds of cells in a squash of a growing root tip, most of them will be in

options.text_md: metaphase, because chromosomes are clearest then
interphase, because it is the longest part of the cell cycle
telophase, because cells spend most time re-forming nuclei

questions.solution_md: Interphase takes up most of the cycle, so most cells in any sample are in interphase — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the G2 phase is correct?

options.text_md: The cell already has double the DNA and prepares the proteins needed for division
The DNA is copied during this phase
The chromosomes line up on the equator

questions.solution_md: G2 follows S, so DNA is already doubled; the cell makes proteins for the spindle and prepares to divide — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A cell in G2 phase has twice as much DNA as a cell in G1 phase.

**Reason (R):** The DNA of the cell is copied in the S phase, which lies between G1 and G2.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and copying of DNA in the S phase is exactly why G2 has double the DNA of G1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the stage of the cell cycle between two divisions, made of G1, S and G2.

answer.model_answer_md: **Interphase.**

questions.solution_md: Interphase.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Prophase, Metaphase, Interphase, Telophase.

answer.model_answer_md: **Interphase**; the others are **stages of mitosis**.

questions.solution_md: Interphase is not a stage of mitosis.

questions.stem_md: A single cell in a plant shoot tip divides by mitosis, and every new cell divides again, three times in all. How many cells are formed?
questions.solution_md: Each division doubles the number: $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ cells.

questions.stem_md: Chromosomes are best counted and studied in which stage of mitosis?
questions.solution_md: At metaphase the chromosomes are most condensed and lie in one plane on the equator — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student sees a cell in which two groups of V-shaped chromosomes are moving towards opposite ends of the spindle. The cell is in
questions.solution_md: Separation of sister chromatids and their movement to opposite poles is anaphase — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which event marks prophase of mitosis in an animal cell?

options.text_md: Sister chromatids move to opposite poles
Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear membrane begins to disappear
A cell plate forms at the centre of the cell

questions.solution_md: Condensing chromosomes, a fading nuclear membrane and centrioles moving apart mark prophase — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In which stage of mitosis do the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear around each group of chromosomes?
questions.solution_md: Telophase reverses prophase: chromosomes uncoil and two nuclei re-form — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why does a dividing onion root cell form a cell plate instead of a furrow?

options.text_md: Its rigid cell wall cannot be pinched inwards

questions.solution_md: A plant cell has a rigid cell wall, so the cytoplasm is divided by a cell plate growing from the centre outwards — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Cytokinesis in a human skin cell takes place by

options.text_md: a furrow in the cell membrane that deepens from outside inwards
a cell plate that grows from the centre outwards
the formation of a new cell wall

questions.solution_md: Animal cells divide their cytoplasm by furrowing (cleavage) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The figure shows four stages of mitosis. In which stage do the chromosomes lie in a single row, each attached to fibres from both poles?
questions.solution_md: Chromosomes lined up on the equator and attached to spindle fibres from both poles is metaphase — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a dividing animal cell, the spindle fibres are organised by the
questions.solution_md: In animal cells the centrioles move to opposite poles and organise the spindle — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? During anaphase of mitosis, each chromosome splits at its centromere and its two chromatids move to opposite poles.
questions.solution_md: True. The centromere divides and the sister chromatids, now daughter chromosomes, move apart.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The two daughter cells formed by mitosis have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

**Reason (R):** In anaphase of mitosis, one chromatid of every chromosome goes to each pole.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the equal sharing of chromatids at anaphase explains why both daughter cells keep the parent number — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Plant cells divide their cytoplasm by forming a furrow from the outside.

**Reason (R):** Plant cells are surrounded by a rigid cell wall.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: plant cells form a cell plate, not a furrow. The reason is true and is why a furrow cannot form — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the division of the cytoplasm after the nucleus has divided.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cytokinesis.**

questions.solution_md: Cytokinesis.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the division of the nucleus during cell division.

answer.model_answer_md: **Karyokinesis.**

questions.solution_md: Karyokinesis.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Root tip, Shoot tip, Anther, Cambium.

answer.model_answer_md: **Anther**; the others are **regions where cells divide by mitosis** (meristems) for growth.

questions.solution_md: Meiosis occurs in the anther to form pollen.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the spindle in a dividing onion root cell forms without centrioles.

answer.model_answer_md: Higher plant cells **lack centrioles**; their spindle is organised from the **polar regions of the cytoplasm**.

questions.solution_md: No centrioles in higher plants.

marking_scheme.step: Lack centrioles; spindle forms from polar cytoplasm

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of mitosis in the correct order and name the stage of the second event: chromatids move to opposite poles; nuclear membrane disappears; chromosomes line up on the equator; nuclear membrane re-forms.

answer.model_answer_md: Order: **nuclear membrane disappears → chromosomes line up on the equator → chromatids move to opposite poles → nuclear membrane re-forms**. The second event (lining up on the equator) is **metaphase**.

questions.solution_md: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between cytokinesis in a plant cell and in an animal cell.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Plant cell: a **cell plate** forms at the centre and grows **outwards**; animal cell: a **furrow** deepens from the outside **inwards**.
2. Plant cell: a **new cell wall** forms between the daughter cells; animal cell: **no wall**, the cell membrane simply pinches in.

questions.solution_md: Cell plate vs furrow; direction; new wall.

questions.stem_md: Draw a neat, labelled diagram of an animal cell with four chromosomes at metaphase of mitosis. Label the centriole, spindle fibre, centromere and chromatid.

answer.model_answer_md: A round cell with a **centriole** at each pole; **spindle fibres** run from both poles to the equator; **four chromosomes** lie in one row on the equator, each shown as **two chromatids** joined at a **centromere** attached to fibres from both poles. No nuclear membrane is drawn.

questions.solution_md: Diagram with chromosomes on the equator and the four labels.

marking_scheme.step: Four chromosomes on the equator, each with two chromatids
Spindle and centrioles at the poles

questions.stem_md: In a human male, meiosis takes place in the

options.text_md: bone marrow, to form blood cells

questions.solution_md: Meiosis occurs only in the reproductive organs while gametes are formed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Homologous chromosomes are a pair of chromosomes that

options.text_md: are the two chromatids of one duplicated chromosome
are alike in size and shape and carry genes for the same characters, one from each parent
carry exactly the same alleles in every case

questions.solution_md: One homologue comes from the father and one from the mother; they carry the same genes, possibly as different alleles — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Crossing over during meiosis results in

options.text_md: a doubling of the chromosome number
new combinations of genes on the chromatids
the formation of the cell plate

questions.solution_md: Exchange of segments between homologous chromatids creates new gene combinations, a source of variation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The body cells of a dog have 78 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will a dog's sperm cell have?
questions.solution_md: Meiosis halves the number: 78 ÷ 2 = 39 — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Meiosis is called a reduction division.

**Reason (R):** Meiosis produces two daughter cells, each identical to the parent cell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true: meiosis halves the chromosome number. The reason is false: meiosis produces four cells that are not identical to the parent — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to ______ (n) in the gametes.
questions.solution_md: Haploid.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the exchange of segments between chromatids of a homologous pair of chromosomes during meiosis.

answer.model_answer_md: **Crossing over.**

questions.solution_md: Crossing over.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Sperm, Ovum, Pollen grain, Skin cell.

answer.model_answer_md: **Skin cell**; the others are **haploid cells formed through meiosis**.

questions.solution_md: A skin cell is diploid and formed by mitosis.

questions.stem_md: Two sisters have the same parents but look quite different. Give two reasons, linked to meiosis, for this variation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Crossing over** between homologous chromosomes forms **new combinations** of genes in each egg and sperm.
2. Homologous chromosomes are **shared out at random** into the gametes, so each sister received a **different mix** of chromosomes.

questions.solution_md: Crossing over; random assortment of homologues.

questions.stem_md: Explain why gametes must have only half the number of chromosomes of body cells.

answer.model_answer_md: At **fertilisation** a sperm and an egg **fuse**. If each carried the full (diploid) number, the zygote would have **double** the normal number, and it would double every generation. Halving keeps the number **constant** from one generation to the next.

questions.solution_md: Fertilisation restores the diploid number.

questions.stem_md: With the help of a labelled diagram, show how crossing over occurs between a pair of homologous chromosomes.

answer.model_answer_md: Draw a **homologous pair**, one chromosome from each parent, each with **two chromatids** joined at a **centromere**. Show two **non-sister chromatids** crossing at a **chiasma** and exchanging segments. Show the result: two chromatids with **mixed segments** (new gene combinations).

questions.solution_md: Pair, chiasma, exchanged segments.

questions.stem_md: A lizard grows back its lost tail. The cell division mainly responsible is

options.text_md: meiosis, which halves the chromosome number
mitosis, which produces many identical cells

questions.solution_md: Regeneration and repair depend on mitosis — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A potato farmer plants pieces of tuber and gets plants exactly like the parent. These new plants are alike because

options.text_md: crossing over is complete in every cell
the new plants grow by mitosis, which keeps the genetic material unchanged
the new plants grow from seeds

questions.solution_md: Vegetative propagation uses mitosis only, so the offspring are genetically identical to the parent — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly distinguishes meiosis from mitosis?

options.text_md: Meiosis produces four cells with half the chromosome number; mitosis produces two cells with the same number
Meiosis produces two identical cells; mitosis produces four
Meiosis occurs in all body cells; mitosis only in gonads
Meiosis keeps the chromosome number; mitosis halves it

questions.solution_md: Four haploid cells versus two diploid identical cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Uncontrolled, repeated mitosis of cells can lead to a tumour.

questions.passage_md:

| Stage | Cells |
|---|---|
| Interphase | 270 |
| Prophase | 15 |
| Metaphase | 6 |
| Anaphase | 5 |
| Telophase | 4 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The root tip has **meristematic cells** that divide actively by mitosis.

**(b)** **Interphase**; it is the **longest** stage of the cell cycle.

**(c)** 10 %

**(d)** (i) **Telophase** (only 4 cells). The two groups of daughter chromosomes reach the opposite **poles** and begin to **uncoil**, becoming thin and less distinct. A **nuclear membrane** and a **nucleolus** re-form around each group, so the cell now has **two nuclei**, and the spindle breaks down.

**OR** (ii) Each centromere **splits** and the sister chromatids are pulled to **opposite poles** by the spindle fibres. This ensures that **each daughter nucleus** gets **one copy of every chromosome**, so both cells have the **same chromosome number** as the parent.

**(e)** A rectangular plant cell with a **spindle**; **four V-shaped daughter chromosomes** moving towards each **pole**, centromeres leading; spindle fibres attached to them. No centrioles (plant cell).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Actively dividing cells.

**(b)** Interphase is longest.

**(c)** Dividing cells $= 15 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 30$; $\dfrac{30}{300} \times 100 = 10$ percent.

**(d)** (i) Telophase: chromosomes uncoil, nuclei re-form.

(ii) Chromatids separate; equal distribution.

**(e)** Anaphase diagram with labels.

questions.passage_md: Arjun scraped his elbow while playing football. Within a week, new skin had covered the wound. His teacher said that the new cells formed by a type of division that copies the cell exactly, after the DNA has been copied in an earlier phase of the cell cycle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Mitosis.**

**(b)** **S phase** (synthesis phase) of interphase.

**(c)** In mitosis each chromosome is **copied** and the two copies (chromatids) **separate equally**, so each daughter cell gets the **same set of chromosomes** and genes as the parent cell.

**(d)** 1. **Growth** of the body from a zygote.
2. **Replacement** of worn-out cells such as red blood cells and the lining of the gut.

**(e)** 1. Skin cell: a **furrow** forms in the membrane; mango cell: a **cell plate** forms.
2. The furrow deepens from **outside inwards**; the cell plate grows from the **centre outwards**.
3. The mango cell lays down a **new cell wall**; the skin cell forms **no wall**.

**(f)** **Centrioles** (centrosome).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Mitosis.

**(b)** S phase.

answer.model_answer_md:
